I’ve been through a lot since my husband passed five years ago, and a few months back, something shifted. For about two months, I felt this relentless energy—like I didn’t need sleep. I’d start reorganizing every cabinet in the house, sign up for three different community classes, and go shopping late at night, buying things I didn’t need—appliances, clothes, even a timeshare I can’t afford. I snapped at my daughter over tiny things, like how she folded the towels. I thought I was helping, but she said I was scaring her.

After that spell passed, I crashed. For the last three months, I can’t get out of bed before 4 a.m., and I just lie there, staring at the ceiling. I don’t want to cook, clean, or even pick out clothes. Deciding what to eat feels impossible. My son mentioned my brother’s suicide when I was young—that was traumatic, yes—but these mood swings, the sleepless rages, the spending… they come and go in waves, not tied to memories. This last bout didn’t follow a flashback or a trigger. They just—hit.
D008-D018_h023.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008-D018_h024.question:
I’ve been feeling really up and down since last year, but the last few months have been especially hard. For about two months, I felt incredible—like I was glowing. I couldn’t sleep, but I didn’t need to; I was choreographing non-stop, dancing ten hours a day, even doing pop-up performances without telling my company. I maxed out two credit cards buying costumes and lighting gear, convinced I was going to start my own dance troupe. My coworkers said I was talking too fast, like my thoughts were skipping.  

Then it crashed. For the past three months, I can’t get out of bed. I don’t enjoy dancing anymore—it feels empty. I lie awake for hours at night, mind foggy, like I’m underwater. Sometimes I get this sudden urge to run into the street or jump off my fifth-floor balcony—not because I want to die, but because it feels like the only thing that would make me *feel* something.  

Yes, I survived a bad accident on tour last year—almost broke my spine—but these highs and lows? They don’t follow that. The dancing frenzy, the spending, the insomnia—they come and go, not tied to flashbacks or triggers. This isn’t fear. This is something else.
D008-D018_h024.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008-D018_h025.question:
I’m a 23-year-old ballet dancer with the city company. For the past two months, I felt like I was glowing—like I could pirouette forever. I wasn’t tired, even when I barely slept. I’d choreograph routines in my head at 3 a.m., call dancers to rehearse, buy costumes and shoes I didn’t need—thousands of dollars gone. It felt amazing, like I finally tapped into my true potential. But before that? For about three months, I couldn’t get out of bed. I’d sleep 12 hours and still feel exhausted. I missed rehearsals, stopped responding to messages, stared at the wall during performances—couldn’t focus on choreography I’d known for years. I kept thinking, “What’s the point? I wish I wouldn’t wake up.”  

Yeah, I’ve had trauma—something happened last year. But the insomnia, the racing thoughts, the spending, the constant motion—it doesn’t happen because of a trigger. It comes out of nowhere, shifts like weather. The trauma lingers, but these highs and lows? They’re not tied to memories or flashbacks. They just *arrive*.
D008-D018_h025.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder
